p.src: It is said that in the reckoning of Heaven and Earth, one cosmic cycle comprises 129,600 years. A cycle is divided into twelve epochs, corresponding to the twelve earthly branches: Zi, Chou, Yin, Mao, Chen, Si, Wu, Wei, Shen, You, Xu, and Hai. Each epoch comprises 10,800 years. Consider the course of a single day: at the hour of Zi the vital force of yang arises, and at Chou the cock crows; at Yin there is not yet light, and at Mao the sun rises; at Chen the morning meal is past, and at Si all things press forward in succession; at Wu the sun stands at the zenith, and at Wei it begins to decline westward; at Shen comes the afternoon meal, the sun sets at You, dusk falls at Xu, and at Hai people settle into rest. Applied to the greater reckoning, when the epoch of Xu reaches its end, Heaven and Earth grow dim and all things cease to flourish. After another 5,400 years, at the beginning of the epoch of Hai, utter darkness reigns and no creature or thing remains between Heaven and Earth; therefore this state is called Chaos. After a further 5,400 years, as the epoch of Hai nears its end, the cycle begins anew at the utmost limit of decline; with the epoch of Zi approaching, light gradually returns. Shao Kangjie said: “At the midpoint of Zi on the winter solstice, the heart of Heaven remains unmoved. It is the moment when the first breath of yang stirs, before the myriad things are born.” At this point, Heaven first takes root. After another 5,400 years, in the midst of the epoch of Zi, all that is light and pure rises upward, and the sun, moon, stars, and constellations come into being. The sun, moon, stars, and constellations are called the Four Signs. Hence it is said: Heaven opened in Zi. After another 5,400 years, as the epoch of Zi nears its end and that of Chou approaches, things gradually become solid. The Book of Changes says: “Great indeed is the primal power of Qian! Supreme indeed is the primal power of Kun! All things owe their birth to it, and thus it obediently bears the will of Heaven.” At this point, Earth first begins to congeal. After another 5,400 years, in the midst of the epoch of Chou, all that is heavy and turbid condenses below, and water, fire, mountains, rocks, and soil come into being. Water, fire, mountains, rocks, and soil are called the Five Forms. Hence it is said: Earth was formed in Chou. After another 5,400 years, when the epoch of Chou ends and that of Yin begins, the myriad things are brought forth. The calendar says: “The breath of Heaven descends, and the breath of Earth ascends; Heaven and Earth unite, and all living things are born.” At this point, Heaven is clear and Earth refreshed, and yin and yang unite. After another 5,400 years, in the midst of the epoch of Yin, human beings, beasts, and birds are born; thus Heaven, Earth, and humanity—the Three Powers—assume their appointed places. Hence it is said: humanity was born in Yin.

p.src: At the very summit of that mountain stood an immortal stone. The stone was three zhang, six chi, and five cun high, and measured two zhang and four chi around. Its height of three zhang, six chi, and five cun corresponded to the 365 degrees of the celestial circuit; its circumference of two zhang and four chi corresponded to the twenty-four seasonal divisions of the calendar. On its surface were nine apertures and eight holes, corresponding to the Nine Palaces and Eight Trigrams. No trees stood on any side to shade it, though fragrant fungi and orchids grew beside it as adornment. Ever since the creation of the world, it had received the pure essence of Heaven, the beauty of Earth, the radiance of the sun, and the splendor of the moon; influenced by them for so long, it gradually became spiritually awakened. Within it an immortal embryo formed. One day the stone burst open and delivered a stone egg as large as a round ball. Touched by the wind, the egg transformed into a stone monkey, complete in every feature and limb. At once it learned to crawl and walk, and bowed to the four quarters. Two beams of golden light flashed from its eyes and shot up to the Palace of the Dipper. This startled the Most Holy, Greatly Compassionate and Benevolent Jade Emperor, the Great Heavenly Venerable, the High Sovereign of the Mysterious Vault, who sat in the Hall of Numinous Heaven within the Cloud Palace of the Golden Gates. He assembled his immortal ministers and, seeing the blaze of golden light, at once ordered Thousand-Mile Eye and Fair-Wind Ear to open the Southern Gate of Heaven and investigate. The two generals duly obeyed the decree and went outside the gate, where they saw clearly and heard distinctly. Presently they returned and reported: “In obedience to Your Majesty’s command, we observed and listened at the source of the golden light. It comes from the borders of the small country of Aolai, east of the ocean in the Eastern Continent of Superior Deity. There stands a Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, and upon it an immortal stone. The stone produced an egg, which transformed into a stone monkey when touched by the wind. The monkey is bowing to the four quarters, and golden light from its eyes shoots up to the Palace of the Dipper. Now that it takes water and food, however, the golden light is gradually subsiding.” The Jade Emperor graciously replied: “That creature below was born of the essential splendor of Heaven and Earth. There is nothing remarkable about it.”

Truly: “In the mountains there is no calendar; winter ends, yet none knows the year.”

p.src: When the monkeys heard this, every one of them was delighted. They all said, “You go first again and lead us inside. Take us in!” The Stone Monkey again closed his eyes and crouched, then leapt inside and called, “Follow me in, all of you! Come in!” The bolder monkeys all jumped through; the timid ones craned their heads and drew back their necks, scratching their ears and cheeks and crying aloud; but after hesitating for a while, they too all went in. Once across the bridge, they snatched at basins and bowls, seized the stove, and fought over the beds, carrying things here and shifting them there. Such was the mischievous nature of monkeys that not one remained still; only when they were utterly exhausted did they stop. The Stone Ape seated himself solemnly above them and said, “Gentlemen, ‘If a man has no trustworthiness, one cannot know what he is good for.’ You said just now that whoever had the ability to enter and leave without injury should be honored as your king. Now I have entered and come out, gone out and entered again, and found this cave heaven where you may sleep in peace and each enjoy the blessings of a settled home. Why do you not honor me as your king?” Hearing this, the monkeys at once bowed low without objection. They arranged themselves by age and rank, paid homage toward the upper seat, and all acclaimed him, “Great King of a Thousand Years!” From that time on, the Stone Ape ascended the throne. p.src: The Handsome Monkey King enjoyed his innocent pleasures for some three to five hundred years. One day, amid a merry feast with the other monkeys, he suddenly grew troubled and began to shed tears. The monkeys hurriedly bowed before him and asked, “Why is Your Majesty distressed?” The Monkey King said, “Though I am in the midst of happiness, I have one concern for the distant future, and that is why I am distressed.” The monkeys laughed again and said, “Your Majesty is truly hard to satisfy. Every day we gather in joy upon this immortal mountain and blessed land, in this ancient cave on a divine continent. We are subject neither to the qilin nor to the phoenix, nor are we constrained by any human throne. We are free and unfettered—this is immeasurable bliss. Why worry about the distant future?” The Monkey King said, “Though today we are beyond the laws of human kings and need not fear the might of birds or beasts, when in years to come we grow old and our blood grows weak, the Lord of Hell will secretly have power over us. Once we die, shall we not have lived in this world in vain, unable to remain forever among the heavenly beings?” When the monkeys heard these words, each covered his face and wept, all now troubled by the thought of impermanence.

p.src: Then from among their ranks a long-armed ape suddenly sprang forth and cried in a ringing voice, “If Your Majesty harbors such concern for the future, then truly the mind that seeks the Way has awakened in you. Among the five orders of living creatures, only three kinds are beyond the dominion of the Lord of Hell.” The Monkey King asked, “Do you know which three kinds they are?” The ape replied, “They are Buddhas, immortals, and divine sages. They escape the cycle of rebirth, are neither born nor destroyed, and live as long as Heaven, Earth, mountains, and rivers.” The Monkey King asked, “Where do these three dwell?” The ape replied, “They dwell here in the world of Jambudvipa, within ancient caves and immortal mountains.” Hearing this, the Monkey King was filled with joy and said, “Tomorrow I shall bid you farewell and descend the mountain. I shall roam to the ends of the seas and journey to the farthest reaches of the earth until I find those three kinds of beings. From them I shall learn the art of ageless immortality and forever escape the calamity imposed by the Lord of Hell.” Ah! These words at once enabled him to leap free of the net of rebirth and caused the Great Sage Equal to Heaven to come into being. The monkeys clapped their hands in praise and all cried, “Excellent! Excellent! Tomorrow we shall cross the ridges and climb the mountains to gather fruits in abundance, and we shall prepare a grand banquet to see Your Majesty off.”

p.src: His fortune had indeed arrived, for after he boarded the wooden raft, strong southeasterly winds blew for days on end and carried him to the northwestern shore, within the territory of the Southern Continent of Jambudvipa. He probed the water with his pole and happened upon a shallow place, so he abandoned the raft and leapt ashore. Along the seashore he saw people fishing, shooting wild geese, digging for clams, and gathering salt. He approached them, played a prank, and pulled a terrifying face, frightening them into dropping their baskets and abandoning their nets as they fled in all directions. He seized one man who could not run fast enough, stripped off his clothes, and imitated humans by putting them on himself. Swaggering along, he passed through provinces and prefectures, learning human manners and human speech in the towns and marketplaces. Eating by day and finding lodging by night, he devoted himself entirely to inquiring after the Way of Buddhas, immortals, and divine sages, seeking a means to attain eternal youth and life. Yet he saw that worldly people all pursued fame and profit, and not one among them cared for the life of his true self. It was just as the saying goes:

p.src: The Monkey King sought the Way of the immortals, but fate granted him no encounter. Throughout the Southern Continent of Jambudvipa, he traversed great cities and visited small counties, and before he knew it eight or nine years had passed. p.src: The Monkey King approached and called, “Venerable Immortal, your disciple salutes you.” The woodcutter hurriedly dropped his axe, turned, and returned the salute. “I am not worthy, not worthy. I am a clumsy fellow who cannot even provide himself with food and clothing. How could I deserve to be called an ‘immortal’?” The Monkey King said, “If you are not an immortal, how could you utter the words of immortals?” The woodcutter asked, “What words of immortals did I utter?” The Monkey King replied, “Just as I reached the edge of the forest, I heard you say: ‘Where kindred spirits meet, each is immortal or a follower of the Way; sitting quietly, they discourse upon the Yellow Court.’ The Yellow Court is a true teaching of the Dao. If you are not an immortal, what are you?” The woodcutter laughed. “To tell you the truth, that song is called ‘Fragrance Filling the Courtyard,’ and an immortal taught it to me. That immortal lives near my humble home. Seeing how hard my household duties were and how I worried day after day, he taught me to recite this song whenever troubles beset me, both to ease my mind and to relieve my weariness. A moment ago I was brooding over some want of mine, so I recited it, never expecting you to overhear me.” The Monkey King said, “Since an immortal lives near your home, why do you not cultivate the Way under him? Would it not be well to learn from him the means of escaping old age?” The woodcutter replied, “My lot has been bitter all my life. My parents raised me from infancy, and just when I had reached eight or nine and begun to understand the ways of the world, my father unhappily died, leaving my mother a widow. I have no brothers or sisters and am all alone, so I have no choice but to attend her morning and evening. Now that my mother is old, I dare even less to leave her. Moreover, our fields and garden lie waste, and we lack food and clothing. I can only cut a couple of bundles of firewood, carry them to market, sell them for a few coins, buy a few measures of rice, cook it myself, and prepare food and drink to support my aged mother. That is why I cannot cultivate the Way.”

p.src: The Monkey King said, “From what you tell me, you are a gentleman who faithfully practices filial duty. Good fortune will surely come to you hereafter. I ask only that you point out the immortal’s dwelling, so that I may go and pay him a visit.” The woodcutter replied, “It is not far, not far. This mountain is called Mount Lingtai Fangcun. Within it stands the Cave of the Slanting Moon and Three Stars, where dwells an immortal known as Patriarch Subhuti. The disciples who have completed their training and departed under that Patriarch are beyond counting, and even now thirty or forty still cultivate the Way with him. Follow that little path southward for some seven or eight li, and you will reach his home.” The Monkey King caught the woodcutter by the arm and said, “Good brother, come with me. If I gain any benefit, I shall never forget the kindness of your guidance.” The woodcutter replied, “You are a most inflexible fellow! I just explained all this to you; do you still not understand? If I went with you, would that not interfere with my livelihood? Who would support my aged mother? I must cut firewood. Go on by yourself, go on.”

p.src: At the sight of him, the Handsome Monkey King threw himself down in worship and kowtowed countless times, crying only, “Master! Master! Your disciple sincerely pays homage, sincerely pays homage!” The Patriarch asked, “Where do you come from? Clearly state your native place and your name before you bow again.” The Monkey King replied, “Your disciple is a native of the Water-Curtain Cave on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, in the Kingdom of Aolai in the Eastern Continent of Superior Body.” The Patriarch shouted an order: “Drive him out! He is clearly a deceitful charlatan. How could such a creature cultivate any attainment of the Way?” The Monkey King hurriedly kowtowed without cease. “Your disciple speaks the honest truth. There is no falsehood or deceit in it.” The Patriarch said, “If you speak truthfully, how can you claim to come from the Eastern Continent of Superior Body? That place is separated from here by two great oceans and the entire Southern Continent of Jambudvipa. How could you possibly have reached this place?” The Monkey King kowtowed and replied, “Your disciple crossed the oceans, landed on distant shores, and wandered from place to place for more than ten years before at last finding my way here.”

p.src: The Patriarch said, “Very well, if you made your way here little by little. What is your surname?” The Monkey King replied, “I have no ill temper. If someone curses me, I do not grow angry; if someone strikes me, I do not lose my temper. I merely offer an apology, and that is the end of it. All my life I have had no ill temper.” The Patriarch said, “That is not the kind of ‘nature’ I mean. What was your parents’ original surname?” The Monkey King said, “I have no parents either.” The Patriarch said, “If you have no parents, I suppose you grew on a tree?” The Monkey King said, “Though I was not born from a tree, I did grow out of a stone. I remember only that there was an immortal stone on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. One year the stone split open, and I was born.” Hearing this, the Patriarch was secretly delighted and said, “By that account, you were fashioned by Heaven and Earth. Get up and walk about, so that I may have a look at you.” The Monkey King sprang to his feet and hobbled back and forth twice. The Patriarch laughed and said, “Though your form is ungainly, you resemble a macaque that feeds on pine nuts. I shall derive a surname from your appearance and have you take ‘Hu,’ the first character of ‘husun.’ Remove the beast radical from the character ‘猢,’ and what remains is ‘古月.’ ‘Gu,’ ancient, signifies old age; ‘yue,’ the moon, signifies yin. Old yin cannot engender or nurture, so it would be better to give you ‘Sun,’ the second character of ‘husun,’ as your surname. Remove the beast radical from the character ‘猻,’ and what remains is ‘子系.’ ‘Zi,’ child, signifies a boy; and ‘xi,’ lineage, signifies the tender young, fitting perfectly with the primal nature of an infant. So I shall give you the surname ‘Sun.’” Hearing this, the Monkey King was overjoyed. He kowtowed before the Patriarch and cried, “Wonderful! Wonderful! Wonderful! Only today have I learned my surname. I earnestly beg you, Master, to show me further mercy: now that I have a surname, please grant me a given name as well, so that I may be properly addressed.” The Patriarch said, “In my school there are twelve characters assigned in sequence for the naming of each generation. You are a junior disciple of the tenth generation.” The Monkey King asked, “What are those twelve characters?” The Patriarch said, “They are Guang, Da, Zhi, Hui, Zhen, Ru, Xing, Hai, Ying, Wu, Yuan, and Jue. In the sequence, your turn falls precisely on the character ‘Wu,’ Awakening. Shall I give you the religious name Sun Wukong?” The Monkey King laughed and said, “Wonderful! Wonderful! Wonderful! From this day forth, I shall be called Sun Wukong.” And so it was:
